In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the histologic differential diagnosis of melanoma is broad and complex.
a lesion that has been diagnosed as melanoma by an experienced dermatologist and/or dermatopathologist should be considered melanoma until proven otherwise.
the diagnosis of melanoma is not a "one size fits all" diagnosis and should not be made on clinical or pathologic grounds without careful consideration of all the available data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the histologic features that distinguish benign from malignant lesions are often not as clear as previously thought.
melanocytic proliferative lesions may be divided into three categories: (a) benign lesions, (b) melanocytic dysplasias (atypical melanocytic hyperlasias), and (c) melanoma.
the diagnosis of melanoma is based on clinical, histologic, and immunohistochemical findings.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the histologic diagnosis of melanoma requires the recognition of atypical cytologic features, such as nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, in the context of an overall architectural pattern that is suggestive of melanocytic proliferation.
a thorough clinical evaluation of a lesion, including the history, physical examination, and dermatoscopic findings, is essential to avoid a misdiagnosis.

, when faced with a difficult histologic diagnosis, one should consider the patient's age, clinical history, and location of the lesion, and then review the histologic features carefully to arrive at an appropriate diagnosis.
